h1: Coasters, table tents and printed collateral that earn their cost
title: Coasters and Print for Brewpubs | Craft Beer School
desc: Which printed pieces earn their cost in an Indian brewpub, from coasters and table tents to menus and takeaway cards and how to design and track them.
teaser: Every printed piece in a brewpub costs money. Some pay it back on the same night. Most are binned by Tuesday.
standfirst: Coasters, table tents, menus and cards are the quiet sales staff of a brewpub. Here is how we decide which pieces earn their print bill and how to make them work harder.
sections: Start with a job for each piece

Every printed piece in a brewpub should have one clear job. A coaster protects the table and keeps the brand in view. A table tent sells one thing this week. The menu helps people choose. A takeaway card brings them back. When a single piece tries to do all of those, it does none of them well.

Before you print, write down the job and how you will know it worked. If you cannot, you probably do not need that piece.

Coasters are the most handled brand item in a brewpub. Guests turn them over, doodle on them and take them home. In a humid Indian taproom, cheap board coasters swell, curl and stick to wet glasses within an hour, so buy proper pulp board made for beer mats and test a few under a sweating glass before you order thousands.

Use one side for your logo in core colours. Use the reverse for something worth reading: a short beer fact, the tap list QR code, a quiz question or an invitation to the next event. Change the reverse a few times a year so regulars see something new.

Count how many coasters you go through in a busy weekend before you set the order size. Guests pocket more than most owners expect, which is good for the brand and bad for a forecast built on table count alone.

A table tent is a small billboard at eye level. Use it to sell one thing: a new beer, a food pairing, a quiz night. Keep it to a headline, an image and a single line of detail. Table tents with a full menu printed on them are rarely read.

The menu is your most important printed piece. Keep beer names, styles, strengths and a short taste line clear and consistent with the brand. Give the beer list space of its own rather than burying it under the food. Print menus in a format you can update cheaply, such as an insert or a reusable holder, because tap lists change. Our guide to taproom design that sells covers where menus and boards sit in the room.

A small card handed with the bill is one of the best value pieces you can print. Put the next event, your growler or takeaway offer where state rules allow it and a QR code to follow you online. Loyalty cards work if the reward is an experience, such as a brewery tour or a tasting, rather than more free beer. Rules on alcohol promotions vary by state, so check what is allowed before you design an offer.

• Use templates. Build reusable layouts for tents and cards so each new one takes minutes, not a designer's day.
  • Stick to the brand book. Same colours, type and voice as your cans and website.
  • Print in sensible runs. Long runs are cheaper per piece but waste money if the content dates. Print evergreen items in bulk and anything with dates or prices in short runs.
  • Choose durable stock. Laminated or wipeable finishes survive spilt beer and cleaning far longer than plain paper.

A few simple tracks tell you which pieces earn their keep. Put a different QR code on each piece and see which one gets scanned. Ask staff which table tents guests mention. Count how many takeaway cards come back for an event. Compare sales of a promoted beer in weeks with and without a table tent.

None of this needs software beyond a free QR generator with scan counts. After a few months, you will know which pieces to reprint and which to drop. Most brewpubs find two or three pieces do almost all the work.

Printed material in a licensed space still needs to follow advertising and promotion rules. Avoid anything that encourages heavy drinking, suggests beer improves performance or appeals to minors. Include a gentle line about not drinking and driving on takeaway cards. These points cost nothing to follow and keep your brand on the right side of the rules.

Printed collateral is one part of how a taproom builds regulars. The bigger picture covers events, community and how all the pieces connect.
faqs: Are custom coasters worth it for a small brewpub?
Usually yes, if you buy proper pulp board and use the reverse for something guests want to read. They are handled more than any other brand item.
How often should we change table tents?
Whenever the thing they sell changes, often every two to four weeks. Old tents for past events make a brewpub look neglected.
How do I know if printed material works?
Use a different QR code on each piece and track scans, ask staff what guests mention and compare sales of promoted beers.
